title: Outer measure and measurable sets
terms: Lebesgue outer measure; Lebesgue measurable set; Caratheodory criterion; sigma- algebra.

exposition.text:
∗
Lebesgue outer measure m (A) is the infimum of the sums of lengths of countable open-interval
covers of A. It is defined for every subset, is monotone and countably subadditive, and may
∗ ∗ ∗
equal infinity. A set E is measurable if m (A) = m (A ∩ E) + m (A \ E) for every A ⊆ R.
Measurable sets form a sigma-algebra: they contain ∅ and are closed under complements and
countable unions, hence countable intersections. Open and closed sets are measurable, and
every subset of a set of outer measure zero is measurable. Arbitrary unions need not preserve
measurability, and not every real subset is Lebesgue measurable.

transforms interval covers and then applies the inverse transformation. This formula needs

∗ ∗
m (A ∩ E) + m (A \ E); measurability requires equality for every test set A.

question.text:
Which operation is guaranteed to preserve Lebesgue measurability for every family of measur-
able real sets?
(A) An arbitrary union, even over an uncountable index set.
(B) Taking every subset of a positive-measure set.
(C) A countable intersection.
(D) Taking an arbitrary image under any function.
(E) Taking the inverse image under any function.

solution.text:
Countable intersections belong to the sigma-algebra. Every real subset is an uncountable
union of measurable singletons, so arbitrary-union closure would incorrectly make all
subsets measurable. Arbitrary functions need not preserve measurability in either direction.

question.text:
∗ ∗
A set A ⊆ R, not assumed measurable, has outer measure m (A) = 2/5. What is m ({7 − 3a :
a ∈ A})?
(A) 2/15
(B) 2/5
(C) 6/5
(D) 33/5
(E) It is undefined unless A is measurable.

solution.text:
Translating a countable interval cover preserves all lengths; multiplying by −3 multiplies
∗
lengths by three. Taking infima gives an upper bound of 3m (A), and applying the in-
verse affine transformation gives the reverse inequality. Thus outer measure scales by the
absolute factor, yielding 6/5, whether or not A is measurable.

question.text:
∗ ∗
A set E ⊆ [0, 1] satisfies m (E) = 3/4 and m ([0, 1] \ E) = 3/4. Which conclusion follows?
(A) E is measurable with measure 3/4.
(B) E is not Lebesgue measurable.
∗
(C) m ([0, 1]) = 3/2
(D) E is countable.
(E) No outer measure can be assigned to E.

solution.text:
If E were measurable, the Caratheodory criterion applied to A = [0, 1] would require 1 =
∗ ∗
m (E) + m (A \ E) = 3/2, a contradiction. Outer measure is defined on every set but is only
subadditive in general; equality across a measurable cut is the additional requirement.

question.text:
If E has outer measure zero, every subset of E is
(A) Countable
(B) Closed
(C) Lebesgue measurable with measure zero
(D) Open
(E) Empty

solution.text:
Monotonicity gives outer measure zero for each subset. Sets of outer measure zero satisfy
the Lebesgue measurability criterion, which is the completeness property of Lebesgue
measure.
